text:
Rafael Mendes: Dropping here for review: component taxonomy v0.3. Open question: do we name the internal “scheduler” as a customer-facing component, or keep it abstracted (e.g., “Capacity & Routing”)?

Christine Wong: +1 on keeping it abstract. “Scheduler” reads like internal implementation. Customers want to know: can requests be admitted / routed / capacity constrained.

Sean Gallagher: Agree. Exposing “scheduler” risks us getting pulled into implementation debates. But we *do* need something that explains 429s / “no healthy backends” / spillover behaviors.

Allison Grant: From metrics POV, we already tag a bunch of this as `scheduler_*` internally, but that doesn’t mean the status page should. We can map alerts -> component without naming the service.

Aisha Bello: Also “scheduler” doesn’t clearly tell them what action to take. “Capacity & Routing” implies: try another region, remove region pinning, fallback model, backoff.

Marissa Cole: Product lens: customers will read “scheduler degraded” and ask “what is that?” We’ll end up with a docs burden and support escalations. “Capacity & Routing” is closer to user mental model.

Paula Mendes: +1. We should make sure the definition is crisp though. “Capacity & Routing” can become a junk drawer if we’re not careful.

Rafael Mendes: The counterpoint I’ve heard: we’ll lose precision. When it’s literally the scheduler / admission control path erroring, the component name should reflect the true failing thing.

Sean Gallagher: We can be precise in the update text without naming the component “scheduler”. Component is the “what customers experience”, not “which binary is on fire”.

Tomáš Novák: :thumbsup: + should keep “Routing” consistent w the runbook examples. If we say “scheduler” on the page, oncall will copy/paste internal terms into updates.

Ethan Park: There’s one wrinkle: some incidents are capacity-only (GPU pool saturation) vs routing-control-plane regression. If they’re both “Capacity & Routing”, does that confuse?

Mina Haddad: Maybe sub-bullets in the component description:
- Capacity constraints (429s, queueing, elevated p95)
- Routing/policy (misroutes, failover not triggering, region-specific admission)
But still one component name.

Christine Wong: Or we split “Capacity” vs “Routing” into two components? I worry that’s too granular for customers. Also, a lot of incidents hit both.

Allison Grant: If we split, we’ll struggle with signal coverage. We don’t have clean alerting boundaries today between “routing policy regressions” vs “capacity saturation.”

Aisha Bello: +1. For now, one component. We can add “region-specific serving” components separately to cover the most common question: which region.

Rafael Mendes: OK. Proposed compromise:
- Public component: “Capacity & Routing”
- In mapping sheet, internally mark as “scheduler/admission-control” as the primary owner service
- In status update template guidance: include symptom + customer action (retry/backoff, use alternate region/model) and avoid internal words
Thoughts?

Sean Gallagher: Works. Also put a line in the mapping guidelines: “Do not mention internal service names (scheduler, router, etc.) unless pre-approved; describe functionally.”

Marissa Cole: + docs snippet in “How to read the status page”: what “Capacity & Routing” means and typical mitigations.

Elliot Price: I can add that to docs. If we keep it customer-language, it’s easier. “Scheduler” would require a glossary and still be confusing.

Paula Mendes: Can we define examples so support can answer “is streaming impacted?” For example, “Capacity & Routing” might mean non-streaming works but streaming retries happen.

Mina Haddad: That’s usually actually “Streaming” component though (disconnects/keepalive). For Capacity & Routing the typical is 429/503 or timeouts before first token.

Allison Grant: Exactly. We should be explicit in the component definition:
- If failures happen before response starts / first token -> Capacity & Routing or API Gateway
- If disconnects mid-stream -> Streaming
This helps keep components from overlapping.

Tomáš Novák: We should capture that in runbook example scenarios. I’ve seen oncall mark “API degraded” for everything.

Rafael Mendes: Great. I’ll update taxonomy doc:
- Replace “Scheduler” with “Capacity & Routing”
- Add definition + examples (429, elevated queueing, admission failures, routing/failover issues)
- Add “don’t say scheduler publicly” note

Sean Gallagher: Decision recorded: public component name = “Capacity & Routing”. Internal = scheduler/admission/routing services as needed. :white_check_mark:

Christine Wong: :+1: Can someone sanity check wording: “We are experiencing capacity constraints and/or routing issues impacting request admission and latency” (too vague?)

Aisha Bello: Maybe: “Some requests are being rate limited or delayed due to capacity constraints and routing control issues.” Then include next update time + mitigation.

Marissa Cole: +1. Avoid “and/or” if possible. We can say “capacity constraints in <region> are causing elevated 429s; routing mitigations in progress.”

Rafael Mendes: Got it. Will incorporate into templates guidance as well (symptoms first, then what we’re doing, then what customers can do).
